title: The Expert in the Loop: Why the Future of AI Isn't Hands-Free
summary: Explore why AI in claims and estimating needs the right context and human expertise to improve workflows, build trust, and support better decisions.
body_markdown:
*In our first two articles, we explored*[how AI can reduce manual work in claims and estimating](https://www.verisk.com/blog/ai-in-estimating-and-claims-workflows-where-efficiency-begins/) *and*[how teams can move from exploration to adoption](https://www.verisk.com/blog/ai-in-property-estimating-workflows-moving-from-exploration-to-adoption/) *. Building on those ideas, we now explore why AI’s value depends on the context and judgment that experienced professionals bring to every claim.*


**


## The first generation of enterprise AI conversations focused on a simple question: What tasks can AI automate?


Today, a more important question is emerging: *How do organizations balance AI, context, and human expertise to achieve better outcomes?*


AI can process information faster than ever before, but speed alone doesn’t create value. Real value emerges when AI is integrated into workflows and supports the people who make decisions.


## How should AI and human expertise share the work?


As AI becomes part of everyday workflows, expectations continue to rise. Many users, and organizational leaders, expect AI to understand situations the way people do, interpreting intent and nuance from a single photo or a few lines of notes. That expectation overlooks the need for context and structure in AI inputs, and critical experience that estimators bring to the table. An estimator who arrives at a loss site brings:


- Knowledge from years of inspections and past losses
- An understanding of what the policyholder is dealing with
- A clear objective for the inspection
- Accountability for the final estimate


AI brings:


- Speed on repetitive tasks
- Pattern recognition across large volumes of data
- Consistency from one file to the next


## Expertise still drives the outcome


Claims decisions depend on context that rarely shows up in a photo. Adjusters and estimators do more than document damage. They decide whether it’s new or pre-existing, and whether to repair or replace.


AI can take much of the administrative load off those decisions. Every hour an estimator doesn’t spend sorting photos or retyping notes goes back to the policyholder and to the complex losses where experience counts most.


The point of AI in this work is to expand what an expert can do in a day.


## Is more context always better for AI?


No. What helps is the right context at the right moment. Give AI too little and its recommendations are generic. Giving it too much context can introduce noise, making it harder to determine what information is most relevant.


Consider an estimator uploading a photo of water-damaged kitchen cabinets. AI can identify base cabinets with swollen particleboard along the toe kick. It can’t see that the dishwasher supply line leaked for three weeks before anyone noticed, or that the same cabinet run continues into the dining area. An estimator who knows those facts will write a different estimate than one working from the photo alone.


The future of AI is not about supplying unlimited information to increasingly capable models. It is about understanding which pieces of context improve outcomes and integrating them naturally into the workflow.


## Learning alongside our users


Better models don’t solve every problem. Some of the most useful feedback we get from XactAI™ users points to the workflow itself. Users tell us when a recommendation appears at the wrong point in a job, or when the AI is missing a detail they already have in hand.


As teams move from pilots into daily use, they judge AI by how well it fits the way they work and whether it helps at the moment they need it. In our experience, that fit affects adoption more than raw model performance.


## Trust drives adoption


Professionals trust AI when they can understand and adjust its recommendations, and when the final call stays with them.


You’ll often hear this described as keeping a “human in the loop.” “Expert in the loop” is more accurate. Adjusters, estimators, contractors, and restoration professionals know the property and the policyholder, and they’re accountable for the result. Their judgment is what makes an AI suggestion worth acting on.


Tools built around that principle earn lasting adoption, because the people using them can see the AI working for them.


## Where AI in claims goes from here


AI creates value when it works alongside experienced professionals, with each element playing a clear role:


- AI supplies speed and scale.
- Context makes the output relevant.
- The expert decides what happens next.


We’re building[XactAI](https://www.verisk.com/resources/campaigns/empowering-the-human-side-of-insurance/) on that principle—because the future isn’t hands-free.
